title: BEFORE JERUSALEM, THERE WAS SHILOH—AND WHAT HAPPENED THERE SHOULD TERRIFY EVERY CHRISTIAN WHO THINKS GOD’S PRESENCE CAN BE TAKEN FOR GRANTED
paragraphs:
BEFORE JERUSALEM, THERE WAS SHILOH—AND WHAT HAPPENED THERE SHOULD TERRIFY EVERY CHRISTIAN WHO THINKS GOD’S PRESENCE CAN BE TAKEN FOR GRANTED
Before David brought the ark to Jerusalem and before Solomon built the Temple, Israel gathered around another sacred place. Its story begins with promise, passes through tears and scandal, and ends with a warning so severe that centuries later God pointed back to Shiloh and said, in effect: Remember what happened there.
There was a time when an Israelite could hear the name “Jerusalem” and not think first of the Temple.
No magnificent house of cedar and stone crowned Mount Moriah.
No worshiper stood in Solomon’s courts.
No pilgrim sang the Songs of Ascents while climbing toward the city that would become inseparable from Israel’s worship.
Before Jerusalem became that place, there was Shiloh.
And if you have ever wondered why Shiloh mattered so much before Jerusalem, the answer is far bigger than geography.

Shiloh became a place where Israel assembled before the LORD. It was associated with the tent of meeting, the distribution of the Promised Land, the ministry of priests, the prayers of a brokenhearted woman named Hannah, the childhood of Samuel, the ark of the covenant—and eventually one of the most sobering demonstrations in Scripture that religious privilege is no substitute for faithfulness to God.
Shiloh’s story is beautiful.
Then uncomfortable.
Then heartbreaking.
And finally, it points beyond itself toward something infinitely greater.
Because Shiloh teaches us that sacred places cannot save sinful hearts.
Religious history cannot substitute for repentance.
Possessing symbols associated with God does not mean that we possess God.
And even Jerusalem itself would eventually discover the same terrifying truth.
But first, we need to return to the beginning.
After Israel entered Canaan, Joshua 18:1 records:
“And the whole congregation of the children of Israel assembled together at Shiloh, and set up the tabernacle of the congregation there. And the land was subdued before them.”
The Hebrew text calls the sanctuary the אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד—’ohel mo‘ed—the “tent of meeting.”
That wording matters.
This was not merely Israel’s national headquarters.
It was associated with meeting before the LORD.
Shiloh stood within the land God had promised Israel, and there the tribes gathered while the remaining territorial inheritances were apportioned.
Imagine the emotional weight of that moment.
Generations earlier, Abraham had lived as a stranger in the land.
Israel had endured slavery in Egypt.
They had witnessed judgment and deliverance.
They had crossed the sea.
They had wandered through the wilderness.
An entire generation had died before entering Canaan.
And now, at Shiloh, Israel stood inside the promise.
The tent was raised.
The tribes assembled.
The land was being distributed.
Shiloh therefore represented more than a location on a map.
It represented arrival.
Promise.
Inheritance.
Worship.
The presence and covenant faithfulness of the God who had brought His people out of bondage.
Long before Jerusalem became the great center of Israelite worship under the monarchy, Shiloh occupied an extraordinary place in Israel’s life.
But Scripture refuses to romanticize sacred history.
And that is where Shiloh becomes painfully relevant to us.
Years pass.
Joshua’s generation fades.
By the opening chapters of 1 Samuel, Shiloh is still associated with worship before the LORD.
Every year, Elkanah travels there with his family “to worship and to sacrifice unto the LORD of hosts in Shiloh” (1 Samuel 1:3).
And walking into this sacred setting comes one of the Bible’s most painfully relatable women.
Hannah.
She is loved, but she is hurting.
She is married, but something inside her feels unbearably empty.
She has endured provocation from her rival.
She weeps.
She cannot eat.
And eventually her anguish becomes prayer.
At Shiloh, Hannah does not arrive pretending she is fine.
She breaks.
First Samuel 1:10 says:
“And she was in bitterness of soul, and prayed unto the LORD, and wept sore.”
The Hebrew expression behind “bitterness of soul” is מָרַת נָפֶשׁ—marat nephesh.
Her pain was not superficial.
This was anguish reaching into the nephesh—the living self, the person, the inner life.
And perhaps this is where Shiloh stops being ancient history.
Because some people reading this know exactly what it means to enter worship carrying something nobody else can see.
You smiled this week.
You answered messages.
You went to work.
You took care of your children.
You posted photographs.
You said, “I’m okay.”
But God heard the prayer underneath the sentence.
Hannah stood before Him with tears instead of performance.
She moved her lips while her voice could not be heard.
And Eli, the priest, misunderstood her.
He thought she was drunk.
Think about that.
A woman is pouring out her soul before God—and the religious authority watching her initially misreads her brokenness.
Some wounds hurt twice.
First because of what happened.
Then because someone misunderstood how badly it hurt.
But Hannah kept bringing her heart before God.
And God remembered her.
Samuel was born.
The child she had prayed for was eventually brought to Shiloh and dedicated to the LORD.
The place that had witnessed Hannah’s tears would now witness Samuel’s growth.
First Samuel 3:1 tells us:
“And the child Samuel ministered unto the LORD before Eli.”
Then comes one of Scripture’s unforgettable nighttime scenes.
Samuel is lying down.
Eli’s eyesight has grown dim.
“The lamp of God” has not yet gone out.
And Samuel hears his name.
“Samuel.”
He assumes Eli called him.
He runs to the old priest.
“I called not,” Eli essentially tells him. “Lie down again.”
It happens again.
Then again.
Finally Eli understands.
This is the LORD.
Samuel returns and waits.
Then:
“Samuel, Samuel.”
And Samuel answers:
“Speak; for thy servant heareth.”
At Shiloh, a new prophetic voice was being raised.
Yet in the same place where Samuel was learning to recognize the voice of God, other men were treating holy things with contempt.
Eli’s sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests.
But Scripture does not protect their reputations simply because they held religious office.
First Samuel 2:12 says:
“Now the sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they knew not the LORD.”
That should stop every religious person in their tracks.
They were around sacred things.
They participated in a sacred system.
They carried sacred titles.
And Scripture says they did not know the LORD.
They abused their priestly position in connection with the sacrifices, and 1 Samuel also condemns their sexual immorality involving women serving at the entrance of the tent of meeting.
The scandal was not outside Shiloh.
It was inside.
And this is one of the recurring warnings of Scripture:
You can stand near holy things while your heart remains far from God.
You can know Christian vocabulary without knowing Christ.
You can own a Bible and resist the God who speaks through it.
You can sing about surrender while protecting the one sin you refuse to surrender.
You can build an audience around Jesus while secretly building a throne for yourself.
You can inherit religious tradition without inheriting living faith.
Shiloh proves that proximity to sacred things is not the same as intimacy with God.
And then the story becomes darker.
Israel goes to war against the Philistines and suffers defeat.
Instead of first responding with humble repentance and seeking the LORD rightly, Israel decides to bring the ark of the covenant from Shiloh.
Their words in 1 Samuel 4:3 reveal the dangerous reasoning:
“Let us fetch the ark of the covenant of the LORD out of Shiloh unto us, that, when it cometh among us, it may save us out of the hand of our enemies.”
Notice the shift.
The ark was associated with the covenant and presence of the LORD.
But Israel began treating it as though possessing the sacred object could guarantee victory.
They wanted the symbol of God’s presence without submitting to the God whose presence the symbol represented.
That temptation did not die in the ancient world.
People still do it.
A cross around the neck.
A Bible on the nightstand.
A Christian verse in the bio.
Church attendance.
Baptism remembered from years ago.
A ministry position.
A famous preacher followed online.
A worship playlist.
None of those things is evil.
Some are beautiful expressions of faith.
But none can replace repentance and living trust in God.
You cannot use Christianity as a lucky charm.
You cannot carry the language of Jesus while refusing the lordship of Jesus and assume everything is fine.
Israel brought the ark into camp.
The people shouted so loudly that the earth rang again.
For a moment, it must have felt like revival.
Noise everywhere.
Religious excitement everywhere.
The enemy was frightened.
Surely victory was coming.
Then Israel was defeated.
Hophni and Phinehas died.
The ark was captured.
When Eli heard what had happened to the ark, he fell backward, broke his neck, and died.
Then Phinehas’s pregnant wife went into labor.
As she was dying, she named her child אִי־כָבוֹד—Ichabod.
First Samuel 4:21 explains:
“And she named the child Ichabod, saying, The glory is departed from Israel: because the ark of God was taken…”
What a devastating ending to a chapter that began generations earlier with a nation gathering around the tent of meeting in the Promised Land.
Promise had become presumption.
Privilege had become complacency.
Priesthood had become scandal.
And people had confused the sign associated with God’s presence with obedience to God Himself.
Shiloh never became Jerusalem.

The ark did not simply return to Shiloh and restore the old order. After its return from Philistine territory, it remained for a long period at Kiriath-jearim, while the biblical story moved toward David, Jerusalem, and eventually Solomon’s Temple.
David later brought the ark to Jerusalem.
Solomon built the Temple.
Jerusalem became the great center of Israel’s worship.
But here is the part many people miss.
God did not allow Jerusalem to become a new religious lucky charm either.
Centuries later, the prophet Jeremiah stood in the gate of the LORD’s house and confronted people who were trusting in the Temple while persisting in sin.
They were effectively saying:
“The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD…”
They thought the existence of the sanctuary guaranteed security.
Then God told them to remember Shiloh.
Jeremiah 7:12 records:
“But go ye now unto my place which was in Shiloh, where I set my name at the first, and see what I did to it for the wickedness of my people Israel.”
That is why Shiloh matters so much.
Shiloh became a warning Jerusalem was commanded to remember.
The message was unmistakable:
Do not presume upon Me because you have My house.
Do not confuse religious privilege with covenant faithfulness.
Do not believe sacred architecture can shelter unrepentant rebellion.
Look at Shiloh.
Psalm 78 similarly looks backward and says that God “forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh” and then traces the story toward Judah and Zion.
Shiloh mattered before Jerusalem partly because its history became a theological warning to Jerusalem.
And Jerusalem eventually fell too.
The Babylonian armies destroyed Solomon’s Temple in 586 BC.
A building could not save a rebellious nation.
But even that is not the end of the story.
Because if the Bible ended with destroyed sanctuaries and sinful people, Shiloh would merely be a tragedy.
Instead, Scripture moves us toward Jesus Christ.
And Jesus does something astonishing.
When confronted over the Temple, He says:
“Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”
John immediately explains:
“But he spake of the temple of his body.”
The Greek word used there is ναός—naos, referring to the sanctuary or temple.
Jesus was pointing beyond stone.
Beyond architecture.
Beyond every earthly sanctuary that could be damaged, corrupted, invaded, or destroyed.
He was pointing to Himself.
Then at the cross, the One who never sinned bore the judgment sinners deserved.
The true scandal of the Gospel is not merely that humanity could become so sinful.
It is that the holy Son of God willingly gave Himself for sinners.
The innocent condemned.
The guilty offered mercy.
The righteous One bearing sins.
The King wearing thorns.
The Creator mocked by creatures.
The hands through whom all things were made pierced by nails.
And the mouth that could have pronounced judgment instead praying:
“Father, forgive them…”
Then He died.
And on the third day, He rose.
This is where every road in this story must finally lead.
Not Shiloh.
Not Jerusalem.
Jesus.
Christianity is not ultimately about finding the correct sacred location.
It is about reconciliation with the holy God through Jesus Christ.
The Gospel does not tell you to hide behind religious symbols.
It calls you to Christ.
The Gospel does not tell you to polish your reputation until God accepts you.
It tells you that sinners must repent and trust in the crucified and risen Savior.
The Gospel does not say your scandal is stronger than His grace.
It says there is forgiveness and redemption in Christ.
Maybe your own life feels like Shiloh.
There was once a season when you felt close to God.
You prayed.
You worshiped.
You meant what you sang.
Then something happened.
Maybe disappointment hardened you.
Maybe secret sin slowly became normal.
Maybe someone in the church wounded you.
Maybe you became very good at looking spiritually alive while privately becoming exhausted.
Maybe your Bible remained open while your heart slowly closed.
Maybe everybody thinks you are doing well.
But you know.
And God knows.
Here is what Shiloh whispers across thousands of years:
Do not confuse yesterday’s encounter with today’s surrender.
And here is what the cross declares louder:
Come home.
Not because your sin does not matter.
It mattered enough for Christ to die.
Not because God simply overlooks rebellion.
He calls you to repentance.
But because Jesus Christ really does receive sinners who come to Him.
There is grace for the ashamed.
Forgiveness for the repentant.
Mercy for the broken.
Restoration for the wandering.
There is no scandal in your history that gives you permission to declare yourself beyond the reach of the Savior.
Peter denied Him.
A thief was crucified beside Him.
Paul had persecuted His people.
Yet grace wrote chapters none of them could have written for themselves.
That does not make sin small.
It makes Christ glorious.
This is why our words, “From Scandal to Grace,” are not merely a slogan.
They describe the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Jesus rewrites everything—not by pretending the old story never happened, but by redeeming people who could never redeem themselves.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, do not perform for the comments.
But do not keep performing before God either.
Let other believers know where they can stand with you.
Your testimony may become the sentence another exhausted believer needed to read tonight.
Not because Shiloh is merely interesting biblical trivia, but because there may come a day when you are tempted to substitute religious familiarity for a living relationship with Christ.
Remember Shiloh then.
Not as a transaction with God.
Not to earn a blessing.
Not because clicking “share” makes you righteous.
Somebody may be hiding behind religion.
Somebody may be Hannah, silently weeping where nobody understands.
Somebody may be Samuel, hearing God calling them back.
Somebody may feel like Ichabod has been written over their entire life—as though the glory is gone and nothing beautiful can ever come again.
They need to know that the story does not end at Shiloh.
It does not even end at Jerusalem.
It ends with our eyes fixed upon Jesus Christ—the crucified Savior, the risen Lord, the only One who can reconcile sinners to God.
Shiloh mattered because God met His people there.
Shiloh mattered because Israel’s inheritance unfolded there.
Shiloh mattered because Hannah wept there.
Samuel listened there.
Priests sinned there.
Judgment came there.
And generations later, Jerusalem was told to look backward and remember.
But Jesus matters infinitely more because every sanctuary before Him was temporary, while He is the risen Lord.
So when everything sacred in your life seems ruined…
when your reputation collapses…
when yesterday’s faith feels painfully distant…
when the consequences finally arrive…
when you discover that religious appearances cannot rescue you…
do not run toward another performance.
Run to Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive the mercy you could never manufacture.
Then get up and follow Him.
Because the most haunting lesson of Shiloh is not simply that sacred places can fall.
It is that we can stand frighteningly close to the things of God while our hearts remain far from God—and still, through Jesus Christ, the repentant sinner can come home.
Your Shiloh may explain how everything fell apart, but Jesus Christ can still determine how your story ends.
